comments.author: Mayoringram
comments.body_html:
FSR 3 in the game is actually FSR 2.2, they slapped in 3 but “3” just like DLSS 3 only added frame interpolation into the package, nothing more and since Tarkov is DX11, it wouldn’t support FG in any way. Anyways, it’d be slightly better if it were to be FSR 3.1 but still a hand optimized algorithm meanwhile XeSS SR (super resolution) and DLSS SR uses AI. That’s why almost every card could use the upsclaing up until FSR 4.

Now thing changed with FSR 4 where it also uses AI just like XeSS SR and DLSS SR. It took them a long ass time to enable for RDNA 3 due to lack of hardware. Simply put, it uses a less accurate algorithm just to work with “INT8” compared to “FP8” acceleration on RDNA 4 (9000 series). But I heard from around that some 9000 series users also started using INT8 version because it’s even lighter for them. Anyway this is the base of it, that’s why FSR up until now sucked ass, it required hand tuning everywhere, could do so little on it’s own.

Sorry for the long post but tried to keep it easy to understand.

comments.author: tenhian-rRrH9
comments.body_html:
Hey matsix, just wanted to share some data from running this on an RX 7800 XT 16G (RDNA3). Been testing on Streets near the 4S area — pretty high load zone, offline no bots.

Some PresentMon numbers from a few sessions:

Quality mode (0.67×, 1707×960 → 2560×1440): FSR4 on vs off — 84.6 vs 84.5 avg FPS. Virtually identical. The bridge overhead shows as ~0.4ms in the built-in debug log (0.13ms actual ffxDispatch, the rest is cross-API fence sync). GPU busy% went from 67% (in-game FSR) to 90% (FSR4 via bridge) — the private D3D12 queue keeps the GPU fed more consistently. Performance mode (0.5×) showed similar results. I also tried Native AA (0.99×): 71 fps with GPU pegged at 100%, which is expected since you’re rendering 2.2× the pixels.

No crashes, no fallback to 3.1.x in any of my sessions. FSR4 4.1.1 stayed active throughout on RDNA3.

On the visual side — the difference is night and day. The in-game “FSR 3” (which is really FSR 2.2 rebranded — the DLL has TryRenderFSR3 reusing FSR2Wrapper with no separate 3.x path) has that characteristic shimmer on chain-link fences, foliage, and distant objects that hand-tuned spatial/temporal filters can’t fix. FSR4’s ML model handles these properly. Things that used to look like paper cutouts now have actual detail.

A couple of environment rendering quirks — terrain normal map pop on open maps like Shoreline, and tree&bush shadows sometimes only partially rendered until you move closer. I’m sure these are either Tarkov’s or FSR4’s characteristics, not the bridge.

Architecturally the interesting thing is the paradigm shift: this takes a game stuck on FSR 2.2’s hand-tuned pipeline and bridges it to an ML-based upscaler through a D3D11→D3D12 interop layer — 0.4ms overhead, no engine changes. The idea of using shared textures + a timeline fence to side-step the API mismatch is a neat solution to a problem that didn’t have an obvious fix. Smart engineering within the constraints.

Thanks for making this.

comments.author: matsix
comments.body_html:
FSR4 can’t be implemented without the way I’m doing it here. I say in more than one place that this can hurt performance. Whether it looks worse or better than FSR3 is subjective. FSR4 is better at cleaning up certain artifacts. FSR3 is better at keeping a sharper image when standing still but it also suffers from noisy artifacts even when standing still.

Also, you’re not technically losing 10-15 fps. It’s not a level graph sort of thing. You’re increasing frame time which means it takes a bit longer to render a frame. If you run at a more CPU intensive area with a lot of bots and enable/disable FSR4 you likely won’t see a change in fps.
